schools.summary: Matthew Henry dwells on the good impressions made: weeping for others' sins may set the senseless weeping for themselves, the congregation a Bochim, a place of weepers, until Shechaniah broke the silence.
Wesley marks how the report of Ezra's grief, dispersed over the city, drew a great company — the influence of great ones' example; Clarke reads the tears as dread of God's displeasure.
Gill notes Ezra had confessed the people's sins with many tears, casting himself down before the house of God.

Clarke: Shechaniah speaks for the people, not himself culpable (cf. James 3:9), 'hope' being miqveh, an expectation of pardon, and Ezra needed just such a chief man's support; Wesley marks his courage in accusing his own house, the hope conditioned on repentance.

Keil and Delitzsch fix the confession's terms, note it moves at once to the covenant remedy, and distinguish this Shechaniah (of Elam) from the descendant of Zattu (Ezra 8:5), holding his father Jehiel distinct from the Jehiel of v.26.
Gill takes Shechaniah for one who came up with Ezra from Babylon and knew the people's temper.

Keil and Delitzsch render the covenant to put away the wives and their children per the counsel of Ezra and those who tremble at the commandment (Ezra 9:4), that all be done according to the law — the deliberate judgment of the godliest, not a private opinion.
Clarke reads nichrath berith as cutting a covenant sacrifice (cf. Genesis 15:10); Wesley insists the children were cast out of the commonwealth but not forsaken, provision being made for them.
Gill takes the covenant as a solemn renewal, binding the assembly afresh by promise and oath to redress the wrong.

themes: a covenant to put away the wives

schools.summary: Clarke grounds Shechaniah's 'we are with thee' in the decree of Artaxerxes (Ezra 7:23ff.), which authorized Ezra and bound every officer to assist him, so that to act is to fulfil his office.
Henry: weeping is good, but reforming is better — the turn from grief to action, a great saint thankful for counsel and courage from an inferior.
Keil and Delitzsch render the rousing appeal — 'up, this concerns thee, we are with thee, be strong and do it' — laying leadership on Ezra yet promising support.
Gill pictures Ezra called to rise from the ground where he lay prostrate in grief.

Keil and Delitzsch note Ezra had continued on his knees through the speech, then arose and made the chiefs of priests, Levites, and all Israel swear to do 'according to this word' — Shechaniah's specific proposal, not a vague penitence.
Clarke: the thing being contrary to their settled practice, Ezra bound them by oath to rectify it, that the work might hold when feeling cooled.
Gill marks Ezra rising from the ground to set about the work at once.
Keil and Delitzsch argue Johanan son of Eliashib is not the high priest of Nehemiah 12:23 (who was Eliashib's grandson, Neh. 12:10) but the namesake of a temple chamber.
Henry reads the fasting as abiding sorrow for sin, kept up till the sin be put away — they struck while the iron was hot.
Wesley has Ezra retire to consult the princes and mourn till something be done; Clarke works the same genealogy, guessing Johanan is the Jonathan/grandson of Eliashib.
Gill notes Ezra departed from before the house of God to the retired chamber.

themes: the transgression of the returned exiles

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch describe the proclamation to all the captivity, issued by the princes and elders, the threatened forfeiture being a devoting of goods to the temple (cf. Leviticus 27:28), not destruction — the reform meaning to gather every offender.
Gill notes the proclamation was made by the voice of a herald throughout the province.
Henry marks the swiftness — they struck while the iron was hot, Ezra summoning all the captivity to Jerusalem under the king's penalties, zeal harnessed to order.
Keil and Delitzsch: the forfeiture is not the destruction of Deuteronomy 13:13ff. but appropriation to the temple, the offender separated from the congregation of exiles.
Clarke: the LXX makes the substance 'anathematized' to a holy use, and the man excommunicated from the Church and exiled from Israel — losing at once his wealth and his place.
Gill reads the three-day limit as forestalling obstruction and preventing the willing from repenting and drawing back.
Henry marks the fitting irony — goods slighting religion given to religion, the contemptuous man excommunicated.

Wesley reads 'Judah and Benjamin' as the whole returned people and the temple-side street as awing them in God's presence, the great rain a token of displeasure; Clarke fixes the ninth month (December) and the winter rain (LXX 'because of the winter').
Keil and Delitzsch place the assembly in the open space by the water-gate (Nehemiah 8:1), the trembling caused by both the grave matter and the drenching rain.
Henry finds a double sign in the rain — judgment on sin, yet the heavens weeping with the penitent (cf. Judges 10:16), and rain that would make the earth fruitful.
Gill includes among the assembled such of the ten tribes as had returned and dwelt among Judah and Benjamin.

themes: a sign of judgment and mercy

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch render the reproof — the strange wives increase Israel's trespass (cf. Ezra 9:6ff.) — and read Ezra's demand as giving glory to God (Joshua 7:19) and separating from the people of the land, i.e., dismissing the wives.
Henry reports Ezra's charge: the marriages threatened to reintroduce the idolatry of the captivity, and he called them to confess, do God's pleasure, and part from idolatrous wives.
Gill sets Ezra standing up in the midst to state the reason for the assembly.

Keil and Delitzsch pair the demand with the answer — the assembly's loud, firm 'as thou hast said, so must we do' — and fix the Hebrew 'upon us' with what follows (cf. Nehemiah 13:13), putting the obligation on the people.
Clarke: confession is acknowledging sin with deep compunction and the fullest resolution to forsake it.
Gill reads the call as open acknowledgment, detestation, and repentance before the God of their fathers.

Clarke weighs the cost — the wives put away, even those with children (v.44), a hardship; yet humanity must have provided for them, no law of God being against humanity — and doubts the reform held, since Nehemiah 13:23 shows the offense recurring.
Gill hears in the loud voice the people's willing, unanimous readiness to comply, so that none could later deny his consent.

themes: the cost to wives and children

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch set out the four grounds — the great gathering, the season of heavy rain, the impossibility of standing without, and that the many cases are no work of a day or two — practical grounds, not excuses.
Henry commends the plan of a standing court over a hurried popular assembly — the delinquents many, hard cases needing deliberation; what is hastily resolved seldom lasts.
Gill reads 'the people are many' of the many guilty of this evil.

themes: too many to judge at once

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch detail the mechanism — the rulers as judicial authority for the whole congregation, offenders coming city by city with their local elders and judges, until God's fierce wrath be turned away.
Wesley: the great council to be settled to determine the causes, local judges best able to inform it of the facts, till the thing be done and God's wrath removed.
Gill takes 'our rulers' as the great court at Jerusalem, constituted as a standing tribunal for the affair.

themes: until the wrath be turned away

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch read the verb as 'stood up against' (cf. 2 Chronicles 20:23) — Jonathan and Jahaziah with two Levites opposed the measure and were overruled — with Rabbi Solomon and Lightfoot, against the Vulgate's 'steterunt super hoc.'
Gill takes the four as those employed to conduct the business — bringing the delinquents in turn, keeping account, preparing the causes.
Wesley agrees they were employed to manage the affair, the two Levites helping to inform the persons concerned in doubtful matters.
Henry records both senses, noting Lightfoot's contrary reading that the four stood against the work, and owning it strange if so great a task met no opposition.

debates.question: Were Jonathan, Jahaziah, and the two Levites the managers of the reform or its opponents?

sides.position: employed to conduct and organize the divorces
they stood up against the measure and were overruled
both readings recorded, the question left open

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch describe the commission — Ezra with heads of fathers' houses, chosen and named for public accountability, set apart and sitting from the first day of the tenth month to examine each case.
Wesley reads 'separated' of the commissioners sequestering themselves from all other business to give themselves wholly to this work.
Gill notes the children of the captivity did as agreed, setting about putting away the strange wives.
Keil and Delitzsch read 'made an end with all' as finishing with the men who had taken strange wives (the idiom of completing a matter, cf. Genesis 44:12), not 'in every place.'
Clarke counts three whole months, tenth month to first, spent examining and making the separations the law required, the calendar framing the labour.
Gill reads the verse as the completed inquiry and examination of all such men.

Keil and Delitzsch identify the four as sons and brethren of the high priest Jeshua (the brethren of the house of Jedaiah, Ezra 2:36), who gave their hands to put away their wives and brought a ram of the flock for a trespass-offering.

Henry weighs the priests' guilt most heavily — they broke the law (Leviticus 21:7) they should have taught — yet credits their penitence in pledging their hands and bringing the trespass-ram (Leviticus 6:6).
Gill: no wonder the evil spread among the people when those who understood the law set such an example.

Keil and Delitzsch open the wider muster — the priestly houses of Immer, Harim, Pashur, then six Levites (of Jeshua and Kadmiel, Ezra 2:40), noting Kelaiah is Kelita and reappears with Jozabad in Nehemiah 8:7 and 10:11.
Clarke reads the given hand as a most solemn pledge, each offering a ram for a trespass-offering in acknowledgment of iniquity.
Gill: they gave their hands, engaging to do it, and actually put away their wives.

Wesley reads 'some had children' as most wives barren by God's providence, and draws the book's lesson — the offense recurs (Nehemiah 13:23), the best reformers can but endeavour, only the Redeemer turns away ungodliness from Jacob (Romans 11:26); Clarke notes the rigour and passes on Justin Martyr's tradition of an Ezra-passover-Saviour passage.
Henry sounds the same note — the recurrence in Nehemiah 13 and Malachi 2:11 shows human reformation imperfect, our hope resting in Christ's atoning blood, not Ezra's court.
Gill closes the count at about a hundred and thirteen men in all found in the trespass.

outliers.note: Passes on Justin Martyr's tradition (Dialogue with Trypho) that Ezra offered a paschal lamb and named the passover the people's Saviour, a passage the Jews are alleged to have expunged — reported as tradition, not fact.

themes: about a hundred and thirteen in all
hope past all human reform, in the Redeemer

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch tally one singer (Eliashib, not the high priest) and three porters (Shallum, Telem, Uri), making ten Levites in all with the six already named (cf. Ezra 2:41ff.).
Clarke marks the register's gradation of classes — priests (v.18), Levites (v.23), singers (v.24) — a descent through the ministering household before the turn to lay Israel.

themes: the ordered classes of the temple

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch reckon some eighty-six lay names in ten families of the return, the sons of Parosh first (cf. Ezra 2:3), and flag the doubled house of Bani as likely a copyist's error.
Clarke (with Calmet) and Wesley read 'of Israel' as the simple Israelites, so named to distinguish the laity from the priests, Levites, and singers.

Keil and Delitzsch survey the ten lay houses and flag the doubled sons of Bani (the second bearing an improbable twenty-seven names, likely a scribe's slip, perhaps for Bigvai), and deny that the Jehiel here is Shechaniah's father.
Wesley identifies the Jehiel among the guilty sons of Elam as Shechaniah's own father (cf. v.2), making the reformer's accusation of his own house a proof of his courage and conscience.

debates.question: Is the Jehiel among the guilty sons of Elam the father of Shechaniah the reformer?

sides.position: the same — Shechaniah accused his own father and house
a different man; the two Jehiels are distinct

themes: the lay houses of Elam and the rest

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch set the sons of Immer among the priestly courses (with Harim and Pashur, cf. Ezra 2:37ff.), who like the house of Jeshua gave their hands and brought a ram of the flock for their trespass, kept house by house for exactness.
Gill's rule governs — no wonder the evil spread when the priests who should have taught the law were themselves ensnared, and not one house only but many.
Henry: the teachers who broke the law emboldened the people, their names recorded to their reproach, yet all submitting to the same discipline and atonement.

themes: no office exempts from the reckoning

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch place these names in the corrupt second listing of the sons of Bani — twenty-seven names too many for one clan, the heading likely a copyist's error (perhaps for Bigvai) — the names genuine, the ascription slipped.
Henry: the names are recorded to their perpetual reproach, yet are also a roll of the reformed, every man having given his hand and submitted.

themes: a roll of shame and of repentance
